lesson.title: The Function Generator: A Voltage Source You Can Shape
lesson.summary: A function generator is an adjustable voltage source that produces repeating waveforms, sine, square, or triangle, whose frequency, amplitude, and offset you can dial in, giving you a known, controllable signal to feed into any circuit you want to study.
lesson.body:
A plain voltage source, like a battery, gives you one fixed value and holds it. A function generator is a voltage source too, but instead of holding a constant level, it is built to output a repeating waveform whose shape, frequency, and size you choose. Set it to produce a sine wave and it behaves like the sinusoidal waveform you have already studied: it has an amplitude (how far the voltage swings above and below its center), a frequency (how many cycles it completes each second), and therefore a period (the time for one cycle), all of which you can adjust with the front panel controls.

Most function generators offer at least three waveform shapes: sine, square, and triangle, selectable with a button, plus separate knobs for frequency, amplitude, and DC offset (which shifts the whole waveform up or down without changing its shape). Because you control every one of these parameters directly, a function generator gives you something a real-world signal rarely offers: a known, repeatable input. If you want to know how a filter circuit responds to a 1 kHz signal, you set the function generator to a 1 kHz sine wave with, say, 2 volts peak to peak amplitude, connect it to the circuit's input, and watch the circuit's output on an oscilloscope.

This pairing, function generator in, oscilloscope out, is the basic setup of nearly every hands on circuits exercise you will do. The function generator supplies a controlled, predictable stimulus; the oscilloscope shows you exactly what the circuit did with it. Even the calibration signal built into most oscilloscopes, a small square wave available at a test pin, is really just a miniature function generator with a fixed frequency and amplitude, and you will use exactly that signal later on when compensating a scope probe.
